{"id": "ba6da328-272b-40ba-abe5-d5999dda1bdd", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Lifecycle rules save money in four ways: they move aging data to cheaper storage classes, delete data you no longer need, clean up hidden storage, and cap old versions. Here are the main ones, roughly by how much they usually save.

## 1. Clean up hidden costs (low risk)
- **Abort incomplete multipart uploads** after 7 days or fewer. Orphaned parts are billed but don't show up in normal object listings.
- **Expire noncurrent versions** on versioned buckets. Old versions pile up silently. You can keep the newest N versions and delete the rest after 30 days.
- **Remove expired delete markers.** This cuts clutter and listing overhead.

## 2. Transition data by access pattern
| Access pattern | Target class |
|---|---|
| Unknown or changing | **Intelligent-Tiering**. It moves objects automatically, has no retrieval fees, and has a small per-object monitoring fee. |
| Infrequent, but needs millisecond access | **Standard-IA** or **One Zone-IA** (One Zone-IA is for re-creatable data only) |
| Archive, rarely read | **Glacier Instant Retrieval**, **Flexible Retrieval**, or **Deep Archive** |

## 3. Expire what you don't need
Delete objects such as logs, temporary exports, and build artifacts after your retention period. Expiration is the biggest saving if the data has no long-term value.

## 4. Watch for these gotchas
- **Minimum object size:** by default, objects under 128 KB aren't transitioned to IA or Glacier classes. Billions of tiny objects can cost more in per-request transition fees than you save. You can filter with `ObjectSizeGreaterThan`.
- **Minimum storage durations:** IA classes charge for at least 30 days, Glacier Instant and Flexible Retrieval for 90, and Deep Archive for 180. Deleting or transitioning an object earlier still bills the full minimum.
- **Transition fees:** each transition is a billed request, so many small objects can erase the savings.
- **Retrieval fees:** IA and Glacier classes charge to read data. Don't tier data that is read frequently.
- **Check the rule's scope:** use prefix, tag, or size filters so a rule doesn't catch data you still need.

## Example rule (JSON)
```json
{
  "Rules": [{
    "ID": "tier-and-expire-logs",
    "Status": "Enabled",
    "Filter": { "Prefix": "logs/" },
    "Transitions": [
      { "Days": 30,  "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
      { "Days": 90,  "StorageClass": "GLACIER_IR" }
    ],
    "Expiration": { "Days": 365 },
    "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": { "NoncurrentDays": 30, "NewerNoncurrentVersions": 3 },
    "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 7 }
  }]
}
```

## Finding where to apply rules
- **S3 Storage Lens** shows which buckets and prefixes hold the most data, noncurrent versions, and incomplete uploads.
- **S3 Storage Class Analysis** recommends when to move data to Standard-IA based on actual access patterns.
- **Cost Explorer**, filtered by usage type, shows whether your spend is storage, requests, or retrieval.

I can inventory your buckets and check which have versioning on, which have no lifecycle configuration, and how much sits in each storage class. That would show you where rules would help most. Tell me if you want that and which account or region to look at.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
